title: Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Animal senses use the same ion channel mechanisms found in bacteria

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: The senses of complex animals (touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc.) are mediated by the same ion channel mechanisms that bacteria already used to sense their world.

fields.label: Work
fields.value: The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Levin M 2019, The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition › The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: Complex animals’ sense of touch, taste, temperature, hearing, etc. are mediated by the exact same ion channel mechanisms that were already discovered by bacteria and used to make sense of their world (Tasneem et al., 2005; Blackwell, 2006; Liebeskind et al., 2012; Nilius and Honore, 2012).

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Levin M, “The Computational Boundary of a "Self": Developmental Bioelectricity Drives Multicellularity and Scale-Free Cognition”, Frontiers in psychology (2019), doi:10.3389/fpsyg.2019.02688; section “The Agent’s Evolutionary Back-Story: Scaling of Information by Bioelectricity”. Scope: Sensory ion channels in animals and their bacterial homologues

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on levin-2019-boundary-14: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.85

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The claim maps to standard comparative sequence and channel-function analyses supported by large public databases. Its universal wording needs interpretation, but broad coverage and direct homolog tests make it resolvable now.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For ion channels mediating each named animal sense, identify bacterial homologues, reconstruct their evolutionary relationships, and compare conserved domains, gating mechanisms, and sensory functions; absence of homologous mechanisms for major modalities would refute the broad statement.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Functional annotation quality varies strongly in bacteria.

Exact same mechanism may mean homology, biophysical principle, or molecular identity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
discriminating power: 0.86
data existence: 0.95
operationalizability: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.8
data adequacy: 0.72

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The cited support for this sentence is comparative genomics of ion channels, and complete proteomes plus family models make that survey a standard analysis. Presence or absence can refute a strict reading for particular senses within weeks. It cannot show that bacterial cells use those proteins as touch, taste, temperature, or hearing in the animal sense. The homology half is open; the identity of sensory mechanism is only partly constrained, so the claim as stated is partially resolvable.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: For the channel families that mediate touch, taste, temperature, and hearing, test bacterial and animal proteomes for homologous sequences and for a shared gating class. Homologs with the same stimulus class in bacteria would support the claim for that sense; a sense whose animal channel has no bacterial homolog, or only a distant fold with a different stimulus, would refute 'the exact same mechanism' for that sense.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Shared folds can gate on different stimuli.

Sequence homology is a proxy for mechanism, not a recording of bacterial taste or hearing.

Some vertebrate sensory proteins, including Piezo and TMC, are weak or absent as bacterial channels.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.8
data existence: 0.8
discriminating power: 0.62
data adequacy: 0.58
analysis feasibility: 0.75

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: For each of the four senses named (touch, taste, temperature, hearing), at least one ion channel that transduces that sense in animals has a predicted structure containing the fold of a known bacterial ion channel, as measured by TM-score, clearly above the score a non-channel membrane protein reaches against the same bacterial channel.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Structures for every protein are predicted with ESMFold2 on the Nebius Scientific AI Platform (single-sequence mode, seed 0) and aligned pairwise with TM-align (tmtools); the TM-score is normalised by the length of the bacterial chain. A sense is 'shared' if some channel listed for it reaches TM >= 0.50 against some bacterial channel AND that score exceeds the GLUT1 negative control's score against the same bacterial channel by >= 0.10. Supports: all four senses shared, with both controls behaving (positive control KCNA2 vs KcsA TM >= 0.50; negative controls myoglobin and GLUT1 below 0.50 against every bacterial channel).

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Refutes: no sense is shared. Mixed: one to three senses shared. Inconclusive (reason 'other'): the positive control scores below 0.50, either negative control reaches 0.50 against any bacterial channel, or every channel listed for a sense has mean pLDDT < 50 (that sense is then reported as undetermined and the verdict is at most mixed).

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'The exact same ion channel mechanisms' is read as shared structural ancestry of the channel protein, the strongest sense in which a mechanism can be 'the same' across 3+ billion years; a shared biophysical principle without homology (e.g. any force-gated pore) would not count. Senses are mapped to the channels that transduce them in mammals: touch to PIEZO2; temperature to TRPV1 (heat) and TRPM8 (cold); taste to OTOP1 (sour), ENaC alpha/SCNN1A (salty) and TRPM5 (sweet, bitter and umami downstream of GPCRs); hearing to TMC1. Monomers are compared because the pore-forming fold lives in a single subunit for all of these families.
